analysis.title: Asset Mini-Cycle
key_insights: Tech will not capture the share of earnings implied by current forecasts, and the equilibrium reached at the end of last week was not sustainable. For tech valuations to hold, the share of revenues from outside the tech complex has to rise, which is hard with energy cost and interest rate headwinds.

To stay risk on from a macro perspective, US profits need to broaden, which TS Lombard thinks is happening. If profit broadening is the condition for risk on, it is time for another rotation into the rest of the economy and for work on who wins and loses from deploying the technology.

If profits fail to broaden, the rest of the economy cannot afford to pay for tech and markets go risk off, with bonds finally catching a break. Alternatively, weak links in the tech chain could break under higher rates, producing a risk off move even if the macro is improving.
TS Lombard still prefers non-US sovereign debt, where there is more to gain if the energy shock reverses. The rise in UST yields has been driven mainly by domestic inflation pressures.

The asset mini-cycle is becoming an established feature of the new regime, which began with a lot of equity after a decade of deleveraging and asset price inflation. Demand resilience keeps investors in risk on, while cost-push shocks periodically crowd capital into tech and the dollar, setting up the next rotation, as long as energy shocks stay small.

A rotation within the US, which is less exposed to the energy drag, looks safer. Any retreat in energy prices is positive for global equities and weakens the dollar. TS Lombard sees little dollar upside from US outperformance at this stage.

Warsh has restored the right-hand side of the dollar smile: the dollar rallies when the US is expected to outperform and the Fed is expected to hike. TS Lombard's hawkish Fed call is now close to priced, and Fed speak appears to be walking back.

TS Lombard expects data to show an overheating economy rather than a need for a couple of insurance hikes: wage growth has bottomed for low income earners and job switchers, and possibly more broadly in AHE excluding education and health. Inflation is not progressing towards 2%. It stands by its call for quarterly hikes.

Dollar hedge ratios have dropped sharply again, leaving dollar investors exposed to another episode of 'post hedging' (dollar negative) if a US-centric shock hits. TS Lombard also flags US risks around the midterms.

The more air that comes out of tech now, the greater the chance of a sustained expansion and real productivity gains. If investors keep inflating a tech bubble, leverage builds from levels that are currently threatening for certain weak links in the AI chain but not systemically problematic, and the problem in one or two years would be larger and more likely to cause a significant recession.
TS Lombard is watching for triggers in the tech space (see Dario's upcoming note) and, short of that, prefers opportunities outside tech.
